clue.text: Playing piano, uncle with FRCS is an accomplished pianist

indicators.note: the letters are 'played' like notes, rearranged into a new tune

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters; 'with' just joins the pieces

explanation.surface: A surgeon uncle turns out to be a gifted pianist when he sits down at the keyboard.
explanation.walkthrough: FRCS (Fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons) looks like an abbreviation to expand, but its four letters go straight into the mix. The answer runs on into 5 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Poulenc, the French composer, was also a fine concert pianist.

clue.text: Badly dressed bum in funny clothing

indicators.note: one piece sits inside another
the outside of 'funny' clothes what goes within

parts.note: only the outer letters of 'funny' do the clothing

explanation.surface: Someone sniffing at a tramp in a ridiculous outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' reads as a vagrant, but it is the backside, RUMP. 'Funny clothing' sounds like the outfit; really it is the shell of the word 'funny'.
explanation.definitionFit: Frumpy describes dowdy, unfashionable dress.

clue.text: Britain draping its leader in part of its coat of arms

indicators.note: draping means hanging around something, so one piece wraps the other

parts.words: part of its coat of arms
parts.note: a lion is one element of the British royal coat of arms
its refers back to Britain, whose leading letter is B

explanation.surface: Britain is pictured hanging a cloak on the figurehead set within its heraldic shield.
explanation.walkthrough: The lion and the unicorn support the royal arms; 'draping' has A LION wrap round B, the first letter of the Britain just named.
explanation.definitionFit: Albion is an ancient and poetic name for Britain, from the white cliffs of Dover.

clue.text: Run Intercity

parts.note: split the word: 'Inter' = put in the grave, and 'city' is the definition

explanation.surface: A railway timetable listing an express service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intercity' is a British brand of fast train, so the clue reads as a single notice; split it into 'Inter' and 'city' and the parts appear.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: split off from 'Intercity', 'city' stands for the Kent cathedral city at the end of a fast line from London.

clue.text: Graceful woman is quiet about work-up

indicators.note: one piece goes round another
in a down clue, a word going up is written backwards

parts.note: to ply a trade is to work at it; sent up it becomes YLP

explanation.surface: A woman keeps quiet about the build-up to a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work-up' looks like one word, a preparation; split it and 'up' turns PLY round.
explanation.definitionFit: A sylph is a slender, graceful girl, after the air spirits of folklore.

clue.text: See 1
Bureaucrat in prison with drug dealer

explanation.surface: An official locked up alongside a drug dealer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In prison' reads as a container instruction, but 'in' only links the definition to the wordplay, and the two pieces sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen-pusher is a desk-bound clerk or bureaucrat.

clue.text: Some without a happy state

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase are used

explanation.surface: Some people go through life without a happy state of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy state' reads as a mood; the state is American and sits across three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Utah is one of the fifty states of the USA, in the Mountain West.

clue.text: Poet in residence seeing difficult birth in early James Bond premieres

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters within the initials
premieres are first showings, so take the first letter of each of early, James and Bond

parts.note: the first letters of these three words, taken together

indicators.note: difficult suggests something awkward or troublesome, so the letters of birth are rearranged

explanation.surface: A writer-in-residence watches a tricky delivery in the first showings of early 007 films.
explanation.walkthrough: 'premieres' takes the initials of 'early James Bond'; 'difficult' jumbles birth, and 'in' sets that jumble between EJ and B. Private Eye magazine's resident poet, E J Thribb, writes mock-solemn obituary verses.
explanation.definitionFit: E J Thribb, aged seventeen and a half, is the spoof house versifier of the satirical magazine Private Eye.

clue.text: My love, never try ear bursting, it's a delicate body part

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
nary is a dialect word meaning not one or never

indicators.note: bursting breaks the letters apart, so try and ear are rearranged together

explanation.surface: A worried sweetheart warns against straining the ears, as they are fragile organs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is an exclamation here, and cor is the British equivalent; 'bursting' breaks up try ear to make the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: A coronary artery supplies blood to the heart muscle, a vital and vulnerable vessel in the body.

clue.text: Top African city describing its environment

indicators.note: in a down or across clue, top here means remove the first letter, as when topping a vegetable

parts.note: Durban is a port city in South Africa

explanation.surface: A leading city in Africa is portrayed by its surroundings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like praise for the city, but it means cutting off its first letter; the definition refers back to the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban is the adjective for town or city settings, so it describes a city's surroundings.

clue.text: Castle at first repaired and newly restored here

definitions.text: Castle at first repaired and newly restored here

indicators.note: take the first letters of the words that follow
the letters are put back together in a new arrangement

parts.note: first letters of Repaired, And, Newly

explanation.surface: A castle freshly repaired and renovated, in the language of a heritage notice.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well as the wordplay: Lancaster Castle, a prison until 2011, has since been restored and opened to visitors. It is also the Lancaster bomber that 14 across needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue describes Lancaster Castle, a prison until 2011 that has since been repaired and opened to visitors.

clue.text: He was bound to catch fire?

definitions.meaning: the surface reads 'he was certain to'; really he was tied down, chained to a rock
the surface reads 'ignite'; really he caught fire as a thief does, stealing it from the gods

explanation.surface: Someone certain to go up in flames.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' reads as 'certain to', and 'catch fire' as ignite. In the myth Prometheus caught (stole) fire from the gods and was bound to a rock as punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Prometheus is the Titan who stole fire for mankind and was chained for it.

clue.text: Architect and writer entertain on vacation

indicators.note: the words are vacated, emptied of everything but their outer letters

explanation.surface: An architect and an author entertaining while away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' sounds like holiday; here it empties both words before it. Fittingly, P C Wren was also a writer (Beau Geste).
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral.

clue.text: Stuck in traffic with no toilets? A disaster

indicators.note: the letters are wrecked and come out in a new order

explanation.surface: The misery of a traffic jam with nowhere to stop for the loo.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a genuine motorist's lament, so 'disaster' reads as a comment rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Nose-to-tail traffic is queued bumper to bumper.

clue.text: One looks for treasure cache, possibly among 10?

indicators.note: among tells us the shuffled letters are placed inside the other piece

parts.note: the answer to 10 across is LANCASTER, a famous wartime bomber aircraft

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of cache could take another order

explanation.surface: A treasure hunter wonders whether a stash might be hidden among a castle's grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 across is the Lancaster, a Second World War bomber; 'possibly' jumbles cache and 'among' sets the result inside BOMBER after its B.
explanation.definitionFit: A beachcomber searches the shore for valuable or interesting things washed up by the sea.

clue.text: Gold disc half lost, oddly no copy of recording

indicators.note: only half the word is kept

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

indicators.note: no odd letters: the 1st and 3rd go, the even ones stay

explanation.surface: A gold disc has lost half its sales and no copies of the recording remain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gold disc' and 'half lost' look like a unit and a phrase; the split falls between them, 'disc half' and 'lost, oddly no'.
explanation.definitionFit: An audiotape is a sound recording on magnetic tape.

clue.text: During break, workers like some bottles of wine

indicators.note: one piece happens inside the span of another

parts.note: a crew is a team of workers

explanation.surface: Staff on their break are partial to a few bottles of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like some bottles' reads as the workers' taste; it is the definition, an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Many modern wine bottles have a screw-top cap instead of a cork.

clue.text: In the morning, perhaps, in case one forgets

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem, marks times in the morning

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of in case might be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A cautious reminder, written in the morning, just in case someone fails to remember.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word but it belongs to the phrase 'In the morning'; 'perhaps' then jumbles the second 'in' with case.
explanation.definitionFit: An amnesiac is a person suffering memory loss, someone who forgets.

clue.text: Dare to break with America's 'special relationship'

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A challenge to Britain to break off its much-vaunted 'special relationship' with the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'special relationship' is the phrase used for the close ties between Britain and the USA; the quotation marks flag it as the definition in a looser sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation marks bend 'special relationship', the political phrase for Anglo-American ties, back to its plain sense: close fellowship between friends.

clue.text: Maroon fibre

definitions.meaning: a verb here: to abandon someone with no way out
a single thread, as of hair or rope

explanation.walkthrough: 'Maroon' looks like a colour; here it is the verb: to strand someone is to maroon them, and a strand is also a fibre.
explanation.definitionFit: Strand means both to leave stranded and a thread.

clue.text: See 8
Not as many start off as pitcher

indicators.note: start off means the first letter is taken away

explanation.surface: Fewer players begin the game than the man throwing the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pitcher' suggests baseball, but it is the jug; 'start off' drops the opening letter of fewer.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large jug with a wide mouth, the kind of vessel also called a pitcher.

clue.text: Nursery doctor coming across outpour in bed

indicators.note: coming across means stretching over, so the doctor's name goes round the other letters

parts.note: Doctor Foster went to Gloucester in the nursery rhyme
read as out + pour: the word pour put out of order, a jumble that the setter folds into one word

explanation.surface: A children's physician visits a patient after a gush of liquid in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outpour' looks like one word, but read it as pour with 'out' signalling a jumble; 'coming across' then has FOSTER, Doctor Foster of the nursery rhyme, spread round the result after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-poster is a bed with a tall post at each corner, often supporting a canopy.

clue.text: Feel sick and so forth, must be admitted to right hospital

indicators.note: one piece is admitted inside the other, like a patient

explanation.surface: A patient feeling sick and worse must be admitted to hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admitted to right hospital' reads as a patient finding the correct ward; the admitting is ETC going into R and H.
explanation.definitionFit: To retch is to heave, as though about to vomit.

clue.text: Fine and even slices of bread and vegetable

indicators.note: the even-numbered letters are sliced out

parts.note: the 2nd and 4th letters of bREAD... b-R-e-A-d

explanation.surface: A lunch of neatly cut bread and vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even slices' sounds like neat cutting; it means the even letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Okra is a green pod vegetable, also called ladies' fingers.

clue.text: Use one's head swiftly when skinny kids start to abstain from food

indicators.note: only the start of 'kids' is used

parts.note: to fast is to go without food

explanation.surface: Quick thinking is needed when thin children start refusing to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swiftly' belongs to the definition: the whole of 'Use one’s head swiftly' is the phrase, and 'start' takes only the K of kids.
explanation.definitionFit: To think fast is to react quickly in the mind.

clue.text: Open space in Casualty

indicators.note: one piece goes inside another

parts.note: A&E, Accident and Emergency, the hospital casualty department

explanation.surface: Room to breathe in a hospital's emergency ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open space' reads as one phrase, a park; split it and 'Open' is the definition. A&E is the British name for a hospital emergency room, once called Casualty (also a TV drama).
explanation.definitionFit: Agape means wide open, as a mouth in surprise.

clue.text: Had a go like crazy in swift mode of travel, etc

indicators.note: in places the shuffled letters within the other word
crazy signals that the letters of had a go like are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone made a frantic attempt during a speedy journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'like crazy' reads as a phrase meaning frantically, but 'like' is part of the letters 'crazy' shuffles, and 'in' puts the result inside PACY, an informal word for fast.
explanation.definitionFit: A package holiday is a trip with travel, hotel and often meals sold together as a single deal.

clue.text: See 27
